output.title: When a rollback drill is worth the time
output.body:
Rollback drills are not about proving that automation is clever. They are about deciding whether you can recover fast enough when it breaks.

For a small business owner, the real question is simple: is this workflow slow or risky to restore if something goes wrong? If the answer is yes, the cost of a rollback drill is usually just the time to design, document, and rehearse the reset before you need it. That is separate from the cost of the failure itself.

I would treat rollback drills as worth the effort for workflows that touch money movement, customer data, or a repeatable multi-step process. Human approval still stays in place for money movement and other high-risk decisions. A drill does not replace that control; it helps you know whether the control can be restored cleanly.

One practical next step: write down the current manual backup process, or identify the single step that would stop the workflow if it failed. Then ask yourself: if this breaks on a Friday afternoon, can I restore it quickly, or will I lose a day to guesswork? If you do not know, the drill is probably worth the setup time. Unglamorous, yes. Useful, also yes.
